strong-acids-bases-s1.title: Four stock solutions
strong-acids-bases-s1.text: A prep room stocks these solutions at 25 °C. Each solute is a strong acid or a strong base.

strong-acids-bases-s2.title: Mixing an acid and a base
strong-acids-bases-s2.text: A student adds 15.0 mL of 0.150 M NaOH to 25.0 mL of 0.120 M HCl in a flask and swirls. Assume the volumes add and the temperature is 25 °C.

strong-acids-bases-s3.title: Four mixtures of HCl and NaOH
strong-acids-bases-s3.html: Key: H₃O⁺ hydronium; OH⁻ hydroxide; Na⁺ sodium ion; Cl⁻ chloride ion. Water molecules are not drawn; at this scale the H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ from water itself are too few to show.

items.q: What is the pH of Bottle 1?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. HNO₃ gives H₃O⁺ directly, so pH = −log(0.0250).

why.correct: HNO₃ ionizes fully, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.0250 M. pH = −log(0.0250) = 1.6021, which is 1.602: three significant figures in the concentration give three decimal places.

items.q: What is the pH of Bottle 2?

mistakes.why: Value: each Ba(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻ ions, so [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.0150 = 0.0300 M.
Value: that is the pOH. Subtract it from 14.00 to get the pH.

items.q: Which bottle has the highest pH?
options: Bottle 2
Bottle 3
Bottle 4
Bottle 1

why.correct: The highest pH goes with the highest [OH⁻]. Bottle 2 has 0.0300 M OH⁻ (pH 12.48); Bottle 3 has 0.0040 M (pH 11.60).
options: Right: two OH⁻ per formula unit makes its [OH⁻] the largest.
KOH gives one OH⁻ per formula unit, so [OH⁻] = 0.0040 M, less than Bottle 2's 0.0300 M.
A very dilute HCl solution is still slightly acidic; its pH is just under 7, not 8.
Bottle 1 is an acid, so its pH is the lowest of the four.

items.q: What is the pH of Bottle 4? (Hint: water itself also supplies H₃O⁺.)

mistakes.why: Value: an acid cannot make water basic. At 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M the acid adds less H₃O⁺ than water already has, so the pH stays just below 7.

why.correct: Water supplies H₃O⁺ too. With x = [OH⁻] from water: [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ + x and (1.0 × 10⁻⁸ + x)(x) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Solving the quadratic gives [H₃O⁺] = 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M, so pH = 6.98, slightly acidic as an acid solution must be.

items.q: A student dilutes 10.0 mL of Bottle 1 to 100.0 mL with water. What happens to the pH?
options: It rises by 1.00 unit
It falls by 1.00 unit
It rises by 10 units
It stays the same, because the moles of acid are unchanged

why.correct: Diluting tenfold makes [H₃O⁺] ten times smaller, 0.00250 M, so the pH goes from 1.602 to 2.602: up by exactly log 10 = 1.00.
options: Right: one factor of ten is one pH unit.
Less H₃O⁺ per liter means a higher pH, not a lower one.
A factor of 10 in concentration is one pH unit, because pH is a log scale.
pH depends on concentration, not on the number of moles; the same moles in more water give a lower [H₃O⁺].

items.q: How many moles of H₃O⁺ are left over after the reaction?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the H₃O⁺ before mixing. The 0.00225 mol of OH⁻ added reacts with it one to one; subtract.

why.correct: HCl: 0.0250 L × 0.120 mol/L = 0.00300 mol H₃O⁺. NaOH: 0.0150 L × 0.150 mol/L = 0.00225 mol OH⁻. They react 1:1, leaving 0.00300 − 0.00225 = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol H₃O⁺. The subtraction leaves the thousandths-of-a-millimole place, so two significant figures.

items.q: What is the pH of the mixture?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by the acid volume only. After mixing, the H₃O⁺ is spread through the total volume, 40.0 mL.
Value: you skipped the neutralization. Subtract the moles of OH⁻ added before finding [H₃O⁺].

why.correct: [H₃O⁺] = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol / 0.0400 L = 0.0188 M. pH = −log(0.019) = 1.727, which is 1.73 (two significant figures in the leftover moles).

items.q: What total volume of 0.150 M NaOH would have to be added to the original HCl to reach the equivalence point?

why.correct: Moles OH⁻ needed = moles HCl = 0.00300 mol; 0.00300 mol ÷ 0.150 mol/L = 0.0200 L = 20.0 mL.
options: Right: equal moles of OH⁻ and H₃O⁺.
That is the volume already added; it leaves acid over.
Equal volumes would be right only if the two concentrations were equal.
This multiplies by the ratio of concentrations the wrong way round: 25.0 × 0.150 / 0.120.

items.q: At the equivalence point of this mixture, what is the pH and why?
options: 7.00, because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ do not react with water
Below 7, because HCl was in the flask first
Above 7, because NaOH was added last
7.00, because no ions are left in the flask

why.correct: At equivalence the flask holds water, Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Neither ion takes a proton from water or gives one to it, so [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] and the pH is 7.00 at 25 °C.
options: Right: both are spectator ions, so the solution is neutral.
The order of mixing does not matter: equal moles of H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ have cancelled.
At equivalence there is no excess NaOH, whatever was added last.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are still dissolved; they just do not change the pH.

items.q: Five HCl and three NaOH formula units were mixed. Which box shows the result?
options: W
X
Y
Z

why.correct: Five HCl give 5 H₃O⁺ and 5 Cl⁻; three NaOH give 3 Na⁺ and 3 OH⁻. Three H₃O⁺ react with the three OH⁻, leaving 2 H₃O⁺, 5 Cl⁻ and 3 Na⁺: Box W.
options: Right: 2 H₃O⁺ left over, and the spectator ions keep their counts.
Box X is the equivalence point: equal numbers of acid and base.
Box Y has excess OH⁻, which needs more NaOH than HCl.
H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ cannot stay side by side in these amounts: they react until one is used up.

items.q: Which box cannot represent a real mixture, and why?
options: Z, because H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ would react until one of them was nearly gone
X, because a solution needs H₃O⁺ ions to conduct electricity
Y, because there are more Na⁺ ions than Cl⁻ ions
W, because there are more Cl⁻ ions than Na⁺ ions

why.correct: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ is tiny, so large amounts of both ions cannot coexist. They react to make water until the product falls to Kw.
options: Right: neutralization goes essentially to completion.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ conduct electricity on their own; X is a neutral salt solution.
Excess NaOH gives more Na⁺ than Cl⁻; Y is a real mixture with base left over.
Excess HCl gives more Cl⁻ than Na⁺; W is a real mixture with acid left over.

items.q: Which box has the highest pH?
options: Y
X
W
Z

why.correct: Only Y has excess OH⁻, so it is basic, with the highest pH.
options: Right: excess hydroxide makes it basic.
X is neutral, pH 7 at 25 °C.
W has excess H₃O⁺, so it is acidic.
Z is not a possible mixture.

items.q: Each ion drawn in Box Y stands for 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol, and the box holds 0.50 L. What is the pH of the mixture?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. Box Y is basic, so pH = 14.00 − pOH.
Value: you used moles as if they were molarity. Divide 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol by 0.50 L first.

items.q: Which of these are strong acids in water? Select all that apply.
options: HBr
HF
HNO₂
H₂CO₃
CH₃COOH

why.correct: Only HBr is on the list of common strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄, H₂SO₄ for its first proton). Select-all items can have a single answer.
options: Right: a hydrohalic strong acid.
HF is the one hydrohalic acid that does not ionize fully in water.
Nitrous acid, HNO₂, is weak; it is nitric acid, HNO₃, that is strong.
Carbonic acid ionizes only slightly.
Acetic acid (vinegar) ionizes only slightly.

items.q: What is the pH of 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M Sr(OH)₂ at 25 °C?

mistakes.why: Value: Sr(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻ per formula unit; double the concentration.
Value: that is the pOH; subtract from 14.00.

items.q: A student pipets 35.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl into a 500.0 mL volumetric flask and dilutes to the mark. What is the pH of the diluted solution?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pH before dilution. Find the new concentration with M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ first.
Value: "dilute to the mark" makes the total volume 500.0 mL; do not add the 35.0 mL on top.

items.q: Solutions of 0.10 M HCl and 0.10 M HNO₃ have the same pH, even though the acids are different. Which explanation is best?
options: Both ionize fully, so each gives 0.10 M H₃O⁺
Both have the same molar mass, so equal moles dissolve
Cl and N have the same electronegativity, so the H–X bonds are alike
Both are diatomic, so they release the same number of protons

why.correct: For a strong acid, [H₃O⁺] equals the acid concentration, whatever the acid. The anion (Cl⁻ or NO₃⁻) is a spectator.
options: Right: full ionization makes the pH depend on concentration alone.
The molar masses differ (36.46 and 63.01 g/mol); the solutions are compared in mol/L anyway.
The two electronegativities are close but the structures differ. What matters here is that both ionize fully.
HNO₃ is not diatomic. Each acid gives one proton per molecule, but that alone does not explain equal pH unless both ionize fully.

items.q: What is the pH after 30.0 mL of 0.0800 M KOH is added to 20.0 mL of 0.100 M HBr?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. The base is in excess, so pH = 14.00 − pOH.
Value: divide the leftover OH⁻ by the total volume, 50.0 mL, not the base volume.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the pH after mixing a strong acid with a strong base in order.
options: Find the moles of H₃O⁺ and of OH⁻ from volume × molarity
Subtract: the smaller amount is used up, the excess remains
Divide the excess by the total volume of the mixture
Convert to pH (through pOH if OH⁻ is in excess)

why.correct: Moles first, because acid and base react by moles, not by concentration. Then the excess, then the total volume, then the log.
